position: both — the cooking sense only before a noun

senses.gloss: Made black by smoke, fire or dirt.
examples: Firefighters walked through the *blackened* remains of the house.
The walls of the old kitchen were *blackened* with soot.
He pulled a *blackened* pan out of the oven.

senses.gloss: Of food, coated in spices and cooked quickly in a very hot pan until dark, in the Cajun style.
senses.ru: обжаренный в специях до тёмной корочки
examples: I'll have the *blackened* catfish with rice.
The restaurant is famous for its *blackened* chicken sandwich.

senses.gloss: Not responsible for anything bad; having done nothing wrong.
examples: The report found that the driver was *blameless*.
Neither side in the divorce was completely *blameless*.
She had lived a quiet, *blameless* life.

senses.gloss: Of food, having very little flavor.
examples: The soup was a little *bland*, so I added some salt.
After the surgery he had to stick to a *bland* diet.
This is the *blandest* salsa I've ever tasted.

senses.gloss: Dull and uninteresting; without strong features or opinions.
examples: The office was painted a *bland* beige.
The senator gave a *bland* statement that said almost nothing.

contrast: The noun is common too: *fill in the blanks*, *my mind drew a blank*. *A blank check* is a signed check with no amount, and figuratively unlimited freedom.

senses.gloss: With nothing written, printed or recorded on it.
examples: Write your answer on a *blank* sheet of paper.
Please don't leave any lines *blank*.
The screen suddenly went *blank*.

senses.gloss: Showing no expression, understanding or memory.
examples: When I asked about the money, he just gave me a *blank* look.
As soon as the test started, my mind went *blank*.

position: attributive only — *a blanket ban*, never *the ban was blanket*
contrast: Much more often a noun (*одеяло*). As an adjective it only comes before a noun and means *applying to everything, with no exceptions* — often with disapproval: *a blanket statement*.

senses.gloss: Applying to all cases or people, without exceptions.
examples: The city imposed a *blanket* ban on fireworks.
That's a *blanket* statement, and it isn't fair to everyone.
The policy offers *blanket* coverage for all employees.

senses.gloss: Making a very loud, harsh noise.
examples: We could hear *blaring* sirens all night.
He drove past with his music *blaring*.
The TV in the waiting room was *blaring*.

senses.gloss: Not impressed or worried by something, often because you have seen it many times before.
examples: New Yorkers are pretty *blase* about celebrities on the subway.
She sounded *blase*, but I could tell she was nervous.
The second time around, I was a lot more *blase* about flying.

contrast: The stress moves: the adjective and the noun are BLAS-fuh-, but the verb *blaspheme* is blas-FEEM.

senses.gloss: Showing disrespect for God or for something religious; humorously, disrespecting something people treat as sacred.
examples: The film was banned in several countries as *blasphemous*.
Some viewers found the painting *blasphemous*.
In Chicago, putting ketchup on a hot dog is about the most *blasphemous* thing you can do.

contrast: *Blatant* is about something bad done openly, without trying to hide it: *a blatant lie*. For something simply easy to see, use *obvious*.

senses.gloss: Very obvious and done openly, without shame.
examples: That was a *blatant* lie, and everyone in the room knew it.
The referee missed a *blatant* foul.
It was the most *blatant* case of discrimination the lawyer had ever seen.

contrast: *The fire was blazing* is usually the verb *blaze*. Before another adjective, *blazing* works like an adverb: *blazing hot*, *blazing fast*.

senses.gloss: Burning strongly and brightly; of the sun or weather, extremely hot.
examples: We sat around a *blazing* campfire.
The players were exhausted after two hours in the *blazing* sun.
It was a *blazing* July afternoon in Phoenix.

senses.gloss: Extremely fast.
examples: The new phone runs at *blazing* speed.
He ran the forty-yard dash in a *blazing* 4.3 seconds.

senses.gloss: Made white or lighter in color by chemicals or by the sun.
examples: She showed up with *bleached* blond hair.
The old fence was *bleached* by years of desert sun.
Some bakers prefer unbleached flour to *bleached* flour.

senses.gloss: Without hope or encouragement.
examples: The future looks *bleak* for the town's last factory.
Doctors gave him a *bleak* prognosis.
Things got even *bleaker* when the funding ran out.

senses.gloss: Of a place or weather, cold, bare and unwelcoming.
examples: The prairie looks *bleak* in the middle of winter.
It was a gray, *bleak* February morning.

senses.gloss: Of eyes, tired and unable to see clearly, especially from lack of sleep.
examples: He looked at me with *bleary* eyes and asked what time it was.
My eyes were *bleary* after staring at the screen all night.
By the end of the flight, the passengers looked even *blearier* than the crew.

senses.gloss: Having tired, red eyes that cannot see clearly, usually after too little sleep.
examples: A few *bleary-eyed* students showed up for the 8 a.m. class.
She came downstairs *bleary-eyed* and went straight for the coffee.
We were all *bleary-eyed* after the overnight drive.

senses.gloss: Made by mixing different kinds or sources together.
examples: This is a *blended* whiskey, not a single malt.
The school uses *blended* learning, with some classes online.
Pour in the *blended* fruit and stir.

senses.gloss: Of a family, made up of a couple and the children from their earlier relationships.
senses.ru: (о семье) смешанная, с детьми от прежних браков
examples: They're a *blended* family with five kids between them.
Holidays can be complicated in *blended* families.

position: both — *blessed with* after a verb; *a blessed relief* before a noun
contrast: The pronunciation follows the meaning. After a verb, *lucky* is one syllable: *We're blessed* (BLEST). Before a noun, *holy* and *welcome* are two: *the Blessed Virgin*, *a blessed relief* (BLES-id).

senses.gloss: Lucky to have something good; given a talent or advantage. Pronounced BLEST.
examples: We've been *blessed* with three healthy kids.
She's *blessed* with a great singing voice.
I feel very *blessed* to have friends like you.

senses.gloss: Holy; connected with God. Pronounced BLES-id.
examples: The church is dedicated to the *Blessed* Virgin Mary.
The pastor quoted the Bible: "It is *more blessed* to give than to receive."

senses.gloss: Bringing welcome relief or happiness. Pronounced BLES-id.
examples: After a week of storms, the sunshine was a *blessed* relief.
The kids finally fell asleep, and there was *blessed* silence.

ru: запущенный, пришедший в упадок; поражённый, загубленный

senses.gloss: Of a city area, run-down, neglected and poor.
examples: The program helps rebuild *blighted* neighborhoods.
The old mill district was one of the *most blighted* parts of the city.
Rows of *blighted* houses stood empty along the street.

senses.gloss: Damaged by disease, or spoiled by something bad.
examples: Farmers had to pull up the *blighted* potato plants.
His career was *blighted* by injuries.

senses.gloss: With a piece of cloth tied over the eyes so that you cannot see.
examples: The *blindfolded* kids took turns swinging at the piñata.
The hostages were kept *blindfolded* for days.
I've made this drive so many times I could do it *blindfolded*.

senses.gloss: So bright that you cannot see.
examples: There was a *blinding* flash, and then the power went out.
Drivers were stuck in *blinding* snow on the interstate.
The sun off the water was *blinding*.

senses.gloss: Very strong or intense.
examples: She woke up with a *blinding* headache.
The car took off at *blinding* speed.

senses.gloss: Extremely happy and peaceful.
examples: We spent a *blissful* week on the beach with no phones.
The first months of their marriage were *blissful*.
It was the *most blissful* nap of my life.

form: -ing from *blister*, as if hot enough to raise blisters

senses.gloss: Extremely hot.
examples: The marathon was run in *blistering* heat.
By noon the sidewalk was *blistering*.

senses.gloss: Very fast.
examples: She set a *blistering* pace from the start.
The band played a *blistering* guitar solo.

senses.gloss: Very angry and critical.
examples: The paper published a *blistering* review of the new restaurant.
The senator launched a *blistering* attack on the plan.

senses.gloss: Casual and unconcerned, in a way that seems careless.
examples: The company showed a *blithe* disregard for safety rules.
He made the *blithe* assumption that someone else would pay.
She was even *more blithe* about the deadline than her boss.

senses.gloss: Happy and carefree; mostly in literary writing.
examples: She had a *blithe* spirit that everyone loved.
The song has a *blithe*, sunny melody.

contrast: For a drain or a nose, Americans more often say *clogged* and *stuffy* (*a clogged drain*, *a stuffy nose*); *blocked* there sounds more British.

senses.gloss: With something in the way, so that nothing can get through.
examples: The road was *blocked* by a fallen tree.
He had surgery to open two *blocked* arteries.
Your number is *blocked*, so my calls won't go through.

senses.gloss: Deep red, like the color of blood.
examples: The sky turned *blood-red* at sunset.
She wore *blood-red* lipstick to the premiere.
The moon looked *blood-red* during the eclipse.

form: compound — *blood* + *curdling*: so frightening it makes your blood go thick

senses.gloss: Extremely frightening, especially of a sound.
examples: We heard a *bloodcurdling* scream from the woods.
The movie has some truly *bloodcurdling* moments.
The noise from the basement was *bloodcurdling*.

position: both — the violence sense mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Done without violence or killing.
examples: The government fell in a *bloodless* coup.
It was a rare *bloodless* revolution.

senses.gloss: Very pale; also without energy or emotion.
examples: His lips were thin and *bloodless*.
Critics called the remake a *bloodless* copy of the original.
Her face went *bloodless* when she heard the news.

senses.gloss: Of eyes, red because the small blood vessels in them are swollen.
examples: His eyes were *bloodshot* from lack of sleep.
She stared at me with *bloodshot* eyes.
Allergies make my eyes itchy and *bloodshot*.

senses.gloss: Marked or covered with blood.
examples: Police found a *bloodstained* shirt in the trunk.
The bandage was *bloodstained* by morning.
The museum displays the general's *bloodstained* coat.

senses.gloss: Eager to kill or hurt people, or enjoying violence.
examples: The story is about a *bloodthirsty* pirate captain.
The crowd grew *bloodthirsty* as the fight went on.
It's one of the *most bloodthirsty* movies of the year.

contrast: In British English *bloody* is also a mild swear word used for emphasis (*bloody hell*). Americans recognize it from British TV but don't use it that way; in American English it means *with blood*.

senses.gloss: Covered in blood or bleeding.
examples: He came home from practice with a *bloody* nose.
Her knees were scraped and *bloody*.
Someone left a *bloody* towel on the floor.

senses.gloss: Involving a lot of violence and killing.
examples: Antietam was the *bloodiest* single day of the Civil War.
The strike ended in a *bloody* clash with the police.

senses.gloss: Covered with uneven patches of color, especially red marks on the skin.
examples: Her face gets red and *blotchy* when she cries.
The cheap paint dried *blotchy*.
The rash was *blotchier* the next morning.

form: compound — from a boxing commentary that describes every punch
contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase, usually without hyphens: *She told us about the fight blow by blow.*

senses.gloss: Describing every detail of an event in the order it happened.
examples: He gave us a *blow-by-blow* account of the meeting.
The book offers a *blow-by-blow* history of the campaign.
I don't need a *blow-by-blow* description, just tell me who won.

form: compound — from the highest-value blue chip in poker

senses.gloss: Of a company or stock, large, well established and reliable.
examples: Her portfolio is mostly *blue-chip* stocks.
Several *blue-chip* companies reported strong earnings.

senses.gloss: Of the highest quality, especially of a sports recruit or a work of art.
examples: The college landed three *blue-chip* recruits this year.
The gallery sells *blue-chip* contemporary art.

senses.gloss: Doing or connected with physical work in factories, construction and similar jobs.
examples: He grew up in a *blue-collar* town in Ohio.
Many *blue-collar* jobs now require technical training.
Her family was proudly *blue-collar*.

senses.gloss: Having blue eyes.
examples: They have a *blue-eyed* baby girl.
Both of her sons are blond and *blue-eyed*.
The poster showed a smiling, *blue-eyed* soldier.

senses.gloss: Of a color between blue and green.
examples: The water in the bay is a clear *blue-green*.
She bought a *blue-green* sweater to match her eyes.
The lake turns *blue-green* in late summer.

form: compound — from the blue ribbon given for first prize

senses.gloss: Of a group, made up of especially qualified or respected people.
examples: The governor appointed a *blue-ribbon* panel to study the problem.
A *blue-ribbon* commission released its report on Monday.

senses.gloss: Of the best quality; having won first prize.
examples: Grandma's *blue-ribbon* apple pie won at the county fair.
They raise *blue-ribbon* cattle.

senses.gloss: Slightly blue.
examples: The screen gives off a *bluish* light.
His lips were turning *bluish* from the cold.
The mountains look *bluish* in the distance.

contrast: For an everyday knife, Americans usually say *dull*; *blunt* is more common in *a blunt object* and *blunt-force trauma*.

senses.gloss: Saying exactly what you think, without trying to be polite.
examples: To be *blunt*, your business plan won't work.
She gave a *blunt* answer to a simple question.
His feedback was even *blunter* than I expected.

senses.gloss: Not sharp; having a rounded or flat edge or point.
examples: The victim was hit with a *blunt* object.
Kids' scissors have *blunt* tips.

senses.gloss: Not clear in shape or outline.
examples: Most of the vacation photos came out *blurred*.
He complained of *blurred* vision after the fall.

senses.gloss: Of a difference or line between things, no longer clear.
examples: The line between work and home has become *blurred*.
With remote jobs, those boundaries are *more blurred* than ever.

contrast: *Blurry* and *blurred* mean nearly the same for pictures and eyesight; *blurry* is the more casual everyday word. Only *blurred* is used for lines between ideas: *blurred boundaries*.

senses.gloss: Not clear; out of focus.
examples: The security footage is too *blurry* to identify anyone.
Everything looks *blurry* without my glasses.
This picture is even *blurrier* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Of weather, with strong, sudden gusts of wind.
examples: It was a cold, *blustery* day in Chicago.
The weekend will be *blustery*, with gusts up to forty miles an hour.
March was *more blustery* than usual this year.

senses.gloss: Talking too proudly about yourself and what you have done.
examples: He's talented but never *boastful*.
The coach was annoyed by the team's *boastful* posts online.
The more he won, the *more boastful* he became.

contrast: An *-ly* word that is an adjective, not an adverb. There is also a separate adverb: *They carried him bodily out of the bar* (by lifting his whole body).

senses.gloss: Relating to the human body.
examples: He was charged with assault causing *bodily* harm.
Doctors monitored all of her *bodily* functions.
Gloves protect nurses from contact with *bodily* fluids.

senses.gloss: Fake or false, though pretending to be real; informally, unfair or wrong.
examples: The website was selling *bogus* concert tickets.
Most of his insurance claims turned out to be *bogus*.
They kicked him out for being late? That's totally *bogus*.

contrast: With a capital letter, *Bohemian* means *from Bohemia*, the region of the Czech Republic. Lowercase *bohemian* (often shortened to *boho* for fashion) describes an artistic, unconventional lifestyle.

senses.gloss: Living in an artistic, unconventional way, without caring about ordinary social rules.
examples: Greenwich Village was once the center of *bohemian* life in New York.
Her apartment has a *bohemian* look, with rugs and plants everywhere.
The neighborhood was a lot *more bohemian* before the rents went up.

senses.gloss: Cooked in boiling water.
examples: I had two *boiled* eggs for breakfast.
Serve the fish with *boiled* potatoes.
Are the peanuts roasted or *boiled*?

senses.gloss: Noisy, energetic and lively.
examples: A *boisterous* crowd filled the stadium.
The kids got *boisterous* after all that cake.
Our table was the *most boisterous* one in the restaurant.

ru: смелый, дерзкий; яркий, насыщенный; жирный (о шрифте)

senses.gloss: Brave and confident, willing to take risks; sometimes too confident to be polite.
examples: The mayor has a *bold* plan to rebuild downtown.
It was one of the *boldest* moves in company history.
If I may be so *bold*, I think you're making a mistake.

senses.gloss: Strong, bright and easy to notice.
examples: She likes *bold* colors like orange and purple.
This coffee has a *bold* flavor.

senses.gloss: Of printed letters, thick and dark.
examples: The key terms are in *bold* type.
Put the headings in *bold*.

contrast: Always capitalized. *A Bolivian*, *Bolivians* are nouns for the people.

senses.gloss: From or connected with Bolivia.
examples: La Paz is the seat of the *Bolivian* government.
My roommate is *Bolivian*.
We tried *Bolivian* salteñas at a café in Virginia.

senses.gloss: Using loud, grand, impressive-sounding language that has little real meaning.
examples: The candidate is known for his *bombastic* speeches.
Critics found the movie's score loud and *bombastic*.
Her tweets got *more bombastic* as the election got closer.

form: Latin for *in good faith*; two words, no hyphen
contrast: Also said boh-nuh-FY-dee. Do not confuse it with the noun *bona fides* (proof that someone is qualified or trustworthy): *She has the academic bona fides for the job.*

senses.gloss: Real and genuine, not fake or pretending.
examples: After one hit song, she became a *bona fide* star.
Is he a *bona fide* expert, or does he just play one on TV?
Only *bona fide* residents can get a parking permit.

senses.gloss: Made honestly and sincerely, without intending to deceive.
examples: The company says it made a *bona fide* offer to the union.
The court decided the sale was *bona fide*.

form: compound — *bone* + *dry*: as dry as a bone

senses.gloss: Completely dry, with no water at all.
examples: After three months without rain, the creek was *bone-dry*.
Check that the wood is *bone-dry* before you paint it.
The turkey came out *bone-dry*, so we covered it in gravy.

senses.gloss: Informal: very stupid.
examples: Leaving the keys in the car was a *boneheaded* mistake.
The coach called the penalty *boneheaded*.
That was the *most boneheaded* play of the whole season.

senses.gloss: Of meat or fish, with the bones removed.
examples: Buy two pounds of *boneless*, skinless chicken breasts.
We ordered a dozen *boneless* wings.
Is the ham *boneless*?

contrast: Informal. It ends in *-s* but is not a plural: *She's bonkers*, never ✗ *a bonker*.

senses.gloss: Informal: crazy, or wildly excited or angry.
examples: You want to drive to Florida tonight? You're *bonkers*.
The fans went *bonkers* when the home team scored.
The price of eggs this year is just *bonkers*.

senses.gloss: Very thin, so that the bones show.
examples: The stray dog was *bony* and scared.
He had long, *bony* fingers.
She was the *boniest* kid in the class.

senses.gloss: Of fish, full of small bones.
examples: Carp is tasty but very *bony*.
I don't like *bony* fish.

contrast: *He was booked* (by the police) is the passive of the verb *book*, *to charge with a crime*, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Of a place, event or person, with all the places or time already reserved.
examples: Every hotel in town is *booked* for the game.
The restaurant is *booked* solid through December.
Sorry, I'm *booked* all week, can we meet Monday?

senses.gloss: Liking reading and study more than sports or social activities.
examples: He was a quiet, *bookish* kid who loved the library.
She's too *bookish* to enjoy loud parties.
Of the two sisters, Emma was the *more bookish* one.

senses.gloss: Growing quickly and very successful.
examples: Austin has a *booming* tech industry.
Business is *booming* this summer.
They opened a shop in the town's *booming* downtown.

senses.gloss: Of a voice or sound, loud and deep.
examples: The announcer has a *booming* voice.
We heard *booming* thunder in the distance.

senses.gloss: Rude and rough in behavior; bad-mannered.
examples: His *boorish* behavior at the wedding embarrassed everyone.
The fans in the upper deck were loud and *boorish*.
He got *more boorish* with every drink.

form: compound — *boot* + *leg*, from hiding bottles in a boot
contrast: Also a noun (*a bootleg of the concert*) and a verb (*to bootleg liquor*). For software, movies and music, Americans more often say *pirated*.

senses.gloss: Made, copied or sold illegally.
examples: During Prohibition, *bootleg* whiskey was sold in secret bars.
Vendors outside the stadium sell *bootleg* T-shirts.
Fans traded *bootleg* recordings of the band's live shows.

senses.gloss: Informal: involving a lot of alcohol, or containing a lot of it.
examples: We had a long, *boozy* brunch on Sunday.
This eggnog is pretty *boozy*.
The office party was *boozier* than anyone expected.

contrast: Before another adjective it works like an adverb: *borderline rude*, *borderline illegal*. As a noun, *the borderline* is the dividing line itself.

senses.gloss: Very close to the line between two categories, so hard to decide; just barely acceptable or just barely a condition.
examples: It was a *borderline* call, but the umpire said he was safe.
Her test scores are *borderline*, so she might not get in.
The doctor said I have *borderline* diabetes.

contrast: *Was born* is the passive of the verb *bear*, not this adjective. Russian *я родился* needs *was*: ✗ *I born in 1990* → *I was born in 1990*. Do not confuse *born* with *borne* (*carried*): *airborne*, *borne by the taxpayer*.

senses.gloss: Having a natural ability for something, as if from birth.
examples: She's a *born* leader.
My grandfather was a *born* storyteller.
You can tell he's a *born* salesman.

senses.gloss: Having become an evangelical Christian through a strong personal religious experience.
examples: He became a *born-again* Christian in his thirties.
Her parents are *born-again* and very involved in their church.

senses.gloss: Newly and very enthusiastic about a belief or activity.
examples: My brother is a *born-again* vegan.
Like many *born-again* runners, she talks about marathons constantly.

contrast: Always capitalized. *A Bosnian*, *Bosnians* are nouns for the people, and *Bosnian* is also the name of the language.

senses.gloss: From or connected with Bosnia and Herzegovina.
examples: St. Louis has one of the largest *Bosnian* communities in the country.
Her grandparents are *Bosnian*.
We had *Bosnian* coffee after dinner.

senses.gloss: Always telling other people what to do.
examples: My older sister was really *bossy* when we were kids.
Nobody wants to work with a *bossy* manager.
He's the *bossiest* person on the committee.

senses.gloss: Connected with plants or the science of plants; made from plants.
examples: We spent the afternoon at the *botanical* garden.
The book has beautiful *botanical* drawings.
The shampoo contains *botanical* extracts.

senses.gloss: Done badly or clumsily, so that it fails or causes damage.
examples: Two men were arrested after a *botched* robbery.
She sued the clinic over a *botched* surgery.
The website launch was completely *botched*.

takes: *by* or *about* + noun; *that*-clause; *to*-infinitive in *can't be bothered to*
contrast: *Bothered* is how you feel; *bothersome* is what causes it. *Can't be bothered (to do something)*, meaning *too lazy to make the effort*, is more British; Americans often say *I don't feel like it*. *Hot and bothered* means *upset* or *sexually excited*.

senses.gloss: Worried, annoyed or upset by something.
examples: I'm not *bothered* by the noise anymore.
Were you *bothered* that he didn't call?
She seemed *more bothered* about the car than about her injury.

senses.gloss: Willing to make the effort; almost always in the negative.
examples: He couldn't be *bothered* to reply to my email.
Some people just can't be *bothered* to recycle.

senses.gloss: Causing annoyance or small problems.
examples: The cough was *bothersome* but not serious.
Mosquitoes are the most *bothersome* part of camping here.
The pop-up ads are getting *more bothersome* every day.

contrast: Always capitalized. In Botswana itself the people are *Batswana* (one person is a *Motswana*), and *Botswana* is often used before a noun: *the Botswana government*. *Botswanan* is the form many American writers use.

senses.gloss: From or connected with Botswana.
examples: The *Botswanan* team won the relay.
Diamonds are a large part of the *Botswanan* economy.
Our guide on the safari was *Botswanan*.

contrast: Much more common as a noun: *at the bottom of the page*. As an adjective it only comes before a noun. *The bottom line* is the final result or the most important fact.

senses.gloss: In the lowest position.
examples: The towels are in the *bottom* drawer.
Sign your name on the *bottom* line.
The cereal is on the *bottom* shelf.

senses.gloss: Lowest in rank, amount or quality.
examples: Students in the *bottom* half of the class got extra tutoring.
Families in the *bottom* 20 percent pay almost no income tax.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase, usually with *from* and no hyphen: *We rebuilt the program from the bottom up.*

senses.gloss: Starting with details or ordinary people and working toward the whole or the leadership.
examples: The company takes a *bottom-up* approach to new ideas.
It was a *bottom-up* movement led by local volunteers.
Economists built a *bottom-up* estimate from store-level sales.

senses.gloss: Extremely deep, or seeming to have no limit.
examples: The canyon looked almost *bottomless*.
Teenage boys seem to have *bottomless* stomachs.
The project became a *bottomless* pit for taxpayer money.

senses.gloss: Of a drink in a restaurant, refilled as many times as you want for one price.
examples: The diner has *bottomless* coffee.
They offer *bottomless* mimosas at weekend brunch.

contrast: The inflatable playhouse that British English calls a *bouncy castle* is usually a *bounce house* in American English.

senses.gloss: Springing back up easily; soft and springy.
examples: The kids love the *bouncy* ball from the dentist.
This mattress is too *bouncy* for me.
Her hair looked *bouncier* after the haircut.

senses.gloss: Lively, cheerful and full of energy.
examples: The song has a *bouncy* beat.
She's always so *bouncy* in the morning.

senses.gloss: Closely connected with something, so that one depends on the other.
examples: Her identity is *bound up* with her work.
The town's history is closely *bound up* with the railroad.
Money problems are often *bound up* with health problems.

senses.gloss: So busy or involved with something that you have no time for anything else.
examples: He was too *bound up* in his own problems to notice.
She's completely *bound up* in the new project.

senses.gloss: Without any limits; seeming to have no end.
examples: The puppy has *boundless* energy.
Her curiosity seems *boundless*.
Settlers crossed the *boundless* prairie in wagons.

senses.gloss: Existing in large amounts; plentiful.
examples: Farmers are hoping for a *bountiful* harvest.
This year's crop was *more bountiful* than last year's.
Thanksgiving dinner was *bountiful*, as always.

senses.gloss: Generous in giving; mostly in formal or religious writing.
examples: They thanked God for his *bountiful* blessings.
The festival was funded by a *bountiful* patron.

contrast: Also stressed at the end, boorzh-WAH. In everyday American speech it is usually a joke or a criticism: *Avocado toast is so bourgeois.* The noun for the class is *the bourgeoisie*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or typical of the middle class, especially in political writing.
examples: Marx wrote about the struggle against *bourgeois* society.
She came from a comfortable *bourgeois* family.

senses.gloss: Too concerned with comfort, money and respectability; conventional.
examples: His artist friends think a house in the suburbs is hopelessly *bourgeois*.
Their tastes got *more bourgeois* as they got richer.
Is a twelve-dollar latte a little *bourgeois*?

senses.gloss: Feeling trapped, with no freedom or no choices.
examples: She felt *boxed in* by her parents' expectations.
The governor is *boxed in* by the budget.
Small apartments make me feel *boxed in*.

senses.gloss: Physically surrounded so that you cannot move out.
examples: My car was *boxed in* by two delivery trucks.
The runner got *boxed in* on the final lap.

senses.gloss: Shaped like a box, square and without curves.
examples: The old Volvo was famous for its *boxy* shape.
That jacket looks a little *boxy* on you.
The new model is even *boxier* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Like a boy, especially looking young and attractive; of a girl or woman, looking like a boy.
examples: At fifty he still has a *boyish* grin.
She wore her hair in a short, *boyish* cut.
He looked *more boyish* without the beard.

senses.gloss: Cold and fresh in a way that makes you feel awake; also, strong and energizing.
examples: We went for a *bracing* walk along the lake.
The water was *bracing*, but we jumped in anyway.
The morning air was even *more bracing* up in the mountains.

senses.gloss: Of water, slightly salty, as where a river meets the sea.
examples: Crabs thrive in the *brackish* water of the bay.
The well water tasted *brackish*.
The river gets *more brackish* closer to the ocean.

contrast: American English says *braid* and *braided* for hair; British English often uses *plait* and *plaited*.

senses.gloss: Twisted together in three or more strands to form one length.
examples: The girl's hair was *braided* for the recital.
He wore a *braided* leather bracelet.
She bought a loaf of *braided* bread for the holiday.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *a brain-dead patient*

senses.gloss: Having no brain activity, though the heart may be kept beating by machines.
examples: Doctors declared him *brain dead* after the accident.
The family agreed to donate the *brain-dead* patient's organs.

senses.gloss: Informal: very stupid, or too tired to think.
examples: After eight hours of exams, I'm completely *brain dead*.
That was a *brain-dead* decision by management.

senses.gloss: Stupid; showing no thought.
examples: It's a fun, *brainless* action movie.
Don't be so *brainless*, check the address first.
Each season of the show gets *more brainless*.

contrast: *He was brainwashed into joining* is the passive of the verb; the adjective describes the state: *brainwashed followers*.

senses.gloss: Made to believe something completely by repeated pressure, so that you no longer think for yourself.
examples: The cult's *brainwashed* members gave away all their money.
Her family thinks she's been *brainwashed*.
You sound totally *brainwashed* by those ads.

senses.gloss: Informal: very intelligent.
examples: She was the *brainy* kid who always finished first.
You don't have to be *brainy* to enjoy the show.
Her little brother turned out to be even *brainier*.

senses.gloss: Browned in fat and then cooked slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot.
examples: The special tonight is *braised* short ribs.
Serve the *braised* cabbage with pork chops.
The lamb is *braised* for four hours.

contrast: *He was branded a traitor* is the passive of the verb *brand*, *to label someone as bad*, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Made or sold under a known company name.
examples: The team store sells *branded* hats and jerseys.
*Branded* drugs cost more than generic ones.
The company gave everyone *branded* water bottles.

senses.gloss: Of an animal, marked with a hot iron to show who owns it.
examples: The rancher counted the *branded* cattle.
*Branded* horses are easier to identify if they're stolen.

senses.gloss: Too confident, loud and aggressive, often in a way that is rude.
examples: The *brash* young CEO promised to beat every competitor.
His style was *brash*, but he got results.
She was the *brashest* player on the team.

senses.gloss: Informal: behaving like a spoiled, badly behaved child.
examples: Stop being so *bratty* and share your toys.
The movie is about a *bratty* rich kid who learns a lesson.
He's the *brattiest* kid on the block.

senses.gloss: Willing to do things that are dangerous or difficult without showing fear.
examples: The *brave* firefighters ran back into the building.
It was *brave* of you to tell the truth.
She's the *bravest* person I know.

senses.gloss: Big, strong and muscular.
examples: Two *brawny* guys carried the piano up the stairs.
The lumberjack had *brawny* arms.
The linemen are *brawnier* than they were a decade ago.

senses.gloss: Open and without shame, about something that should cause shame.
examples: Thieves stole the car in a *brazen* daylight robbery.
His lies were so *brazen* that people almost believed them.
It was one of the *most brazen* art thefts in history.

senses.gloss: Easy to break.
examples: Put anything *breakable* on the top shelf, away from the kids.
Mark the box "*breakable*" before you ship it.
We packed the *breakable* dishes in towels.

form: compound — from the phrasal verb *break away*
contrast: Also a noun, especially in hockey and soccer: *He scored on a breakaway.*

senses.gloss: Having left a larger group, country or organization to form a separate one.
examples: Fighting broke out in the *breakaway* region.
A *breakaway* group of members started a new church.
The *breakaway* league signed several star players.
